1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	Vision-language-action models (VLAs) fine-tune pretrained language models on robot demonstrations to produce actions from visual observations and language instructions~\cite{brohan2023_rt2,kim2024_openvla}, but which of the resulting representational changes reflect action training and which are inherited from the pretrained backbone?
5	In these decoder-only architectures, image tokens precede instruction tokens, and the causal attention mask restricts multimodal integration to a single readout token~\cite{wang2025seeing,pei2025rethinking}; how representations at this critical position are reshaped by action fine-tuning remains unknown.
6	
7	Behavioral studies show that VLAs exhibit visual dominance~\cite{grant2026} and underweight instructions~\cite{haon2025}, but existing representational analyses target single architectures.
8	No prior work tests whether instruction routing---the internal mechanisms by which instruction tokens influence action-relevant representations---is consistent across backbone families or decomposes training-associated effects from inherited base-model priors.
9	
10	We address this gap with a cross-architecture analysis of three VLAs (OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024_openvla}, TraceVLA~\cite{zheng2024tracevla}, and NORA~\cite{hung2025nora}) across four LIBERO~\cite{liu2023_libero} task suites (\S\ref{sec:setup}).

Before testing cross-architectural generality, we establish core phenomena on OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024_openvla} (Appendix~\ref{sec:openvla_deepdive_appendix}).
At L1, instruction-dominant heads form a gradient: random initialization 0/32, Llama-2 base 9/32, VLA-trained 24/32.
Per-layer $R^2$ probing (Figure~\ref{fig:action_r2_threecond}) reveals a corresponding gradient: the trained model peaks at L9 ($R^2 = 0.643$), Llama-2 base declines steadily from L0, and random initialization collapses to negative $R^2$ at deep layers.
All three conditions share L0 ($R^2 = 0.645$), so divergence arises from Transformer processing: pretrained weights preserve action-decodable structure while random weights produce destructive interference, and VLA training builds on this pretrained scaffold rather than constructing representations from scratch.
These phenomena motivate the cross-architecture tests that follow.

We define $R^2$ exit collapse as $\Delta R^2 = R^2_{\text{peak}} - R^2_{\text{exit}}$, the drop in action-probe decodability from peak layer to exit layer (Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_matrix}).
VLM-to-VLA fine-tuning is associated with substantial exit collapse across all tested conditions: TraceVLA~\cite{zheng2024tracevla} $\Delta R^2 = 0.156$--$0.362$ across all four suites, and NORA~\cite{hung2025nora} $\Delta R^2 = 0.308$ (Spatial) and $0.455$ (Goal) (Figure~\ref{fig:r2_collapse}), all exceeding the $\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ threshold for substantive collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_arch_analyses}).
Under VLA-to-VLA conditions, OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024_openvla} shows only small fluctuations across all four suites ($\Delta R^2 = 0.033$--$0.086$, all below $0.10$); reference baselines similarly show $\Delta R^2 \leq 0.097$.
The gap between the largest non-collapse value ($0.097$) and smallest collapse value ($0.156$) spans $0.059$; any threshold in this interval yields identical grouping, and a permutation test rejects random label assignment ($p = 0.008$; Appendix~\ref{sec:delta_r2_threshold}).
Even excluding NORA-Goal (whose bootstrap CI is unreliable; Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_matrix}, footnote $b$), the remaining VLM-to-VLA values span $\Delta R^2 = 0.156$--$0.362$, consistently exceeding the $0.10$ threshold.
Monte Carlo cross-validation supports this separation: VLM-to-VLA trained CIs lie entirely above zero (lower bounds $\geq 0.09$), while VLA-to-VLA trained CIs span or nearly span zero (Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_matrix}).

\paragraph{Instruction Sensitivity in Action-Producing VLAs}
We first evaluate counterfactual sensitivity in action-producing models using a shared action-space metric.
Across OpenVLA and TraceVLA, instruction perturbations produce medium-to-large action divergence in all eight architecture-suite cells (Figure~\ref{fig:counterfactual_bar}).


\looseness=-1
Every perturbation yields $d = 0.45$--$1.52$ (summary in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:cf_summary}; full rankings in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:counterfactual}).
The ``empty'' condition ranks first in 6/8 cells; ``paraphrased'' ranks last in 7/8, indicating encoding beyond token-level matching.
TraceVLA produces systematically higher effect sizes ($d = 0.97$--$1.52$) than OpenVLA ($0.45$--$1.21$).
Same-metric comparison in two OpenVLA cells shows training increases sensitivity on Spatial but the OXE-pretrained model exceeds the LIBERO-trained model on Long-Horizon ($d = 1.05$ vs.\ $0.57$), consistent with broader instruction responsiveness in the general-purpose model.
\textbf{Instruction perturbation produces graded action divergence with effect sizes reflecting semantic distance.}

Counterfactual sensitivity (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}) confirms that trained VLAs use instruction content, but does not reveal whether this reliance originates from training or from backbone priors.
L1 attention profiling addresses this by comparing head routing before and after VLA fine-tuning.
TraceVLA's reference (Phi-3-Vision) saturates at 32/32 heads before VLA training; training slightly reduces this to 27--30/32.
NORA's reference (Qwen2.5-VL) allocates 13--14/16; training leaves this unchanged at 12--13/16.
OpenVLA shows 24--26/32 in the OXE-pretrained baseline with similar trained values (Figure~\ref{fig:cross_arch_l1}).
\textbf{L1 instruction routing is an inherited backbone property, not a consequence of VLA training.}

\subsection{Representation Extraction}
\looseness=-1
From each architecture, we extract hidden states at every transformer layer from two token positions: (a)~\textbf{image\_mean}, the mean activation over image tokens, and (b)~\textbf{readout}, the hidden state at the final pre-action token, which follows both image and instruction tokens in the causal sequence and can attend to all preceding context.
L0 denotes the embedding layer output, L1 through L$N$ the hidden states after each transformer layer ($N = 32$ for OpenVLA and TraceVLA, $N = 36$ for NORA), with the final layer including the output layer norm.
In all three architectures, image tokens precede instruction tokens; the causal mask prevents image tokens from attending to instructions by construction.

\looseness=-1
We cross two factors in a $2 \times 2$ factorial design: \emph{training status} (trained vs.\ reference) and \emph{instruction presence} (with vs.\ without task description), applied to all 10 available cells in the cross-architecture matrix.
OpenVLA additionally provides representations from the DinoSigLIP projector output (4{,}096-D), DINOv2 and CLIP external baselines, and the branch-split before fusion; these sources support the OpenVLA deep-dive analyses (\S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}).

L0 denotes the embedding layer, L1--L$N$ the post-transformer hidden states ($N = 32$ for OpenVLA/TraceVLA, $36$ for NORA).

tool_args.old_string:
\paragraph{Action probes.}\looseness=-1
To quantify how much action-relevant structure is accessible at each layer, we train two-layer MLP probes~\cite{alain2017} to predict 7-DoF action vectors from frozen representations (architecture and training details in Appendix~\ref{sec:openvla_methods_appendix}).
We report probe $R^2$ as a measure of action decodability.
Higher $R^2$ indicates that actions are more accurately predictable from that representation under the probe; it should not be interpreted as evidence that the model causally uses that layer for action generation.
We define $\Delta R^2$ as the difference between the maximum layer-wise $R^2$ and the exit-layer $R^2$, and use $\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ as a descriptive threshold for substantial peak-to-exit reduction.
Train/test splits follow demonstration boundaries (demo-level splitting reduces $R^2$ from $0.7$--$0.9$ to $0.4$--$0.6$ vs.\ random splitting; Appendix~\ref{sec:delta_r2_threshold}).
95\% CIs are obtained via Monte Carlo cross-validation ($n = 1{,}000$ iterations) with demo-level resampling; the canonical peak layer is fixed from the full-data split to avoid winner's-curse bias.
Linear probes yield consistent patterns (Appendix~\ref{sec:linear_probe}).

\paragraph{Action probes.}\looseness=-1

$\Delta R^2 = R^2_{\text{peak}} - R^2_{\text{exit}}$; we use $> 0.10$ as the threshold for substantial peak-to-exit reduction.

\paragraph{Concurrent work.}
Fang et al.~\cite{fang2026when} construct a behavioral benchmark of counterfactual instruction failures on LIBERO; their evaluation measures \emph{whether} the model follows the correct instruction, while our perturbation measures \emph{how much} hidden-state geometry changes (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}).
Buurmeijer et al.~\cite{buurmeijer2026} probe low-level motor features in OpenVLA; instruction-level routing is the focus of our analysis.
Concurrent work addresses visual representation collapse~\cite{kachaev2025dont} and instruction information collapse~\cite{lian2026bayesianvla} during VLA fine-tuning; our $\Delta R^2$ metric offers a complementary diagnostic for measuring such collapse across architectures.
We additionally distinguish training-associated from inherited effects across three architectures, a decomposition absent from prior single-architecture studies.
tool_args.new_string:
\paragraph{Concurrent work.}
Fang et al.~\cite{fang2026when} evaluate VLA instruction-following behaviorally; our analysis measures representational change (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}).
Buurmeijer et al.~\cite{buurmeijer2026} probe low-level motor features in a single VLA; we focus on instruction-level routing across three architectures.
Concurrent work on visual~\cite{kachaev2025dont} and instruction information collapse~\cite{lian2026bayesianvla} in VLAs is complementary; our $\Delta R^2$ metric offers a cross-architecture diagnostic.

tool_args.content:
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

\looseness=-1
Across three backbone families, our analyses consistently decompose VLA instruction routing into training-associated effects (exit collapse, counterfactual sensitivity) and inherited base-model priors (L1 attention routing).
This decomposition enables practical diagnostics: $\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ flags under-utilized exit-layer representations without rollouts, and mid-layer features offer principled tap points for downstream reward models and planners.
The cross-architecture consistency suggests these are general properties of autoregressive VLA fine-tuning; extending this analysis to non-autoregressive action heads and closed-loop validation is a natural next step.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\looseness=-1
Our conclusions rest on $N{=}2$ VLM-to-VLA transitions plus one VLA-to-VLA case, all causal decoders on a single benchmark (LIBERO); flow-matching~\cite{black2024_pi0} and diffusion~\cite{ghosh2024_octo} action heads may behave differently.
All findings are correlational ($R^2$ measures decodability, not causal reliance); the $\Delta R^2$--success-rate correlation ($\rho{=}0.583$, $p{=}0.10$; Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}) is underpowered ($n{=}9$); each architecture is analyzed at a single trained checkpoint.
All evaluations are open-loop---the link between $\Delta R^2$ and task performance remains indirect.
The counterfactual sensitivity metrics differ between action-producing models (Cohen's $d$) and reference VLMs (cosine distance), preventing direct cross-condition comparison.
Extending to additional VLAs, non-autoregressive action heads, and closed-loop behavioral validation are priorities for future work.
